To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) object representations for multiple visual object categories overlap in lateral extrastriate cortex (LOC); 2) a common neural substrate for view-invariant object recognition is present in LOC and in medial FG; 3) the view-invariant object representations in medial FG show a relative preference for face representations, whereas LOC is category-invariant; 4) the view-invariance in LOC is not limited to the category of chairs; and 5) the view-invariable representations in
repetition effects for multiple object identities in LOC and medial FG are independent of changes in viewpoint.

(i) repetition effects for multiple object identities are found in the right medial fusiform gyrus and in lateral occipito-temporal cortex; (ii) these effects are category-independent; and (iii) they are present regardless of whether the objects have the same or different viewpoint and retinal size.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the brain maintains representations of visual objects across different views.
the neural processes underlying view-independent recognition of visual objects, which is a key question in visual neuroscience.
how visual object representations are maintained across changes of viewpoint and size.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

view-invariant recognition of objects is mediated by a distributed network of regions, with a relative preference for face processing in the medial fusiform gyrus and for nonface objects in the lateral occipital cortex.
view-invariant representations of visual objects overlap in extrastriate cortex and are not restricted to a single subregion for each category.

view-invariant recognition for multiple visual categories is supported by a distributed network of object-selective regions in extrastriate cortex, including both category-selective regions and regions that respond to multiple object categories, and that these object-selective regions can support view-invariant recognition, but with varying degrees of category selectivity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neural processes underlying view invariant recognition are not category specific and that they involve a distributed network of brain regions including LOC and medial fusiform.
the medial FG, which was originally thought to be face-selective, is actually more general and is more likely to be the object category-selective area.
there is a category-independent representation for visual objects in LOC and medial FG, and a category-dependent representation for faces in lateral FG.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the neural processes underlying the maintenance of visual object representations across changes in viewpoint do not depend on distinct subregions within visual cortex for distinct object categories, but rather involve a common neural substrate for multiple visual categories.
the view-invariance problem is a general one for multiple categories of visual objects and that it involves the same regions of extrastriate cortex for multiple categories.
view-independent recognition for multiple objects relies on a common neural substrate, which is located in lateral occipito-temporal cortex.
